Both rulers prioritized personal luxury over statecraft while the treasury remained entirely empty [PDF p. 302]. Isaac II alienated provincial populations by selling imperial offices and permitting unchecked extortion [PDF p. 302]. He subsequently lost Bulgaria and Cyprus to sustained native rebellions [PDF p. 303]. His brother Alexius III seized power through a calculated palace coup in 1195 [PDF p. 304]. Alexius III demonstrated singular energy only during this usurpation and proved equally incompetent in diplomatic and military affairs [PDF p. 304]. The imperial military structure had already collapsed following earlier Seljuk invasions and widespread mercenary reliance [PDF p. 301].

Venetian commercial interests later diverted the Fourth Crusade toward Constantinople [PDF p. 305]. Crusader leaders agreed to restore the blind Isaac II to the throne after his son Alexius promised substantial financial subsidies [PDF p. 306]. The invading forces successfully breached the sea defenses in 1203 through naval engineering innovations [PDF p. 308]. Alexius III abandoned the capital while his restored son proved incapable of meeting the promised obligations [PDF p. 308]. Popular unrest subsequently erupted when the young emperor seized church plate to satisfy Western creditors [PDF p. 310]. A military usurper named Alexius V murdered the imperial heirs and assumed the throne [PDF p. 310]. The Crusaders launched a second siege in April 1204 and captured the weakened city after a decisive naval assault [PDF p. 313]. Frankish soldiers then systematically plundered Constantinople for three days [PDF p. 315]. Baldwin of Flanders subsequently established a Latin Empire that quickly proved unsustainable [PDF p. 318].

Greek resistance rapidly consolidated into three successor states centered at Nicaea, Trebizond, and Epirus [PDF p. 324]. Theodore Lascaris successfully defended Nicaean territory against both Frankish and Turkish incursions [PDF p. 324]. Michael Paleologus later usurped the Nicaean throne and consolidated Greek military power at the battle of Pelagonia [PDF p. 329]. He recovered Constantinople in 1261 after discovering the Latin garrison entirely unprepared for defense [PDF p. 330]. The restored Paleologan empire immediately faced severe commercial decline and territorial fragmentation [PDF p. 333]. Venetian merchants permanently displaced Byzantine control over Levantine trade routes [PDF p. 335]. Michael VIII disbanded native provincial militias and relied upon foreign mercenaries to prevent internal coups [PDF p. 338].

Andronicus II compounded these structural weaknesses by hiring the violent Grand Company of mercenaries [PDF p. 342]. These troops subsequently devastated Thrace and eventually settled as rulers in Athens [PDF p. 343]. Turkish forces concurrently exploited Byzantine military neglect to conquer substantial portions of Asia Minor [PDF p. 344]. Andronicus II further weakened the realm by engaging in a prolonged dynastic conflict with his grandson [PDF p. 345]. Andronicus III ultimately assumed sole authority in 1328 and fought desperately against advancing Ottoman forces [PDF p. 346]. The Ottoman emir Orkhan systematically captured Bithynian strongholds and institutionalized the Janissary infantry corps [PDF p. 348].

The author attributes this prolonged decline primarily to systematic administrative failure rather than external conquest alone [PDF p. 335]. Future scholarship requires more balanced regional analysis to fully explain the rapid territorial fragmentation.
